reason: The provided sources fully support a surprising 45-second story with well over 10 verified multi-sourced claims about the OSIRIS-REx sample capture incident.
story: When NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on asteroid Bennu, it was almost too successful. The probe pressed its robotic arm against the surface and fired a burst of nitrogen gas to stir up dust and pebbles. But it didn't just grab a handful—it scooped up so much material that rocks jammed the collector head's mylar lid wide open. Precious asteroid dust began spilling out and drifting away into the vacuum of space. Realizing that any further movement or a planned weighing spin could cause them to lose the entire harvest, mission controllers hastily canceled tests and rushed to secure the overflowing sample inside the return capsule. Despite the chaotic leak, the probe still brought home a record-shattering 121.6 grams of asteroid material—over double the mission requirement.
angle: The spacecraft grabbed so much asteroid material that rocks jammed its lid open, causing valuable samples to drift off into space.

claims.claim: The spacecraft touched down on asteroid Bennu on October 20, 2020.
OSIRIS-REx collected so much material that rocks jammed the sampler head's sealing mylar flap open.
Collected asteroid material began to slowly escape and drift away into space through the jammed seal.
The mission team canceled a planned post-sampling spinning maneuver to determine sample mass because it would result in more sample loss.
The team decided to expedite the sample stowing procedure, securing the head on October 27 or 28, 2020.
The sample return capsule landed at the Utah Test and Training Range on September 24, 2023.
The total recovered asteroid material weighed 121.6 grams (4.29 ounces).
OSIRIS-REx is NASA's first asteroid-sampling mission and the first US spacecraft to return samples from an asteroid.
The primary mission cost approximately US$800 million.
Upon contact, a burst of nitrogen gas was released to blow regolith particles into the sampler head.
The sample return capsule was transported to NASA's Johnson Space Center for processing.

disputed: Sources give slightly varying estimates of the exact amount of sample lost before stowing (e.g., tens of grams versus general flakes drifting), but all agree a massive surplus remained safely inside the head exceeding requirements. Scripts should state generally that some material was lost before the seal was secured.
